Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results A fourth undersea fiber-optic cable serving Vietnam has developed a fault, further disrupting international Internet connectivity with three other cables remaining out of service. The SJC2 cable, which connects Vietnam with other parts of Asia, developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, on Tuesday, according to an international undersea cable operator. The simultaneous problem with four undersea cables has badly affected Vietnam's international Internet traffic, the operator said. The AAE-1 cable has been experiencing problems in its S1.H2 segment since February and has yet to be repaired. The Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the U.S., and the Intra Asia (IA) cable are also experiencing problems, with repairs expected to begin in early September. Undersea fiber-optic cables carry the bulk of Vietnam's international Internet traffic, and so its international bandwidth has been substantially reduced. Internet service providers have been balancing loads, rerouting traffic and adding capacity through other connections to minimize the impact on users. Ethernet cables connected to the LAN ports of a Wi-Fi modem/router. Photo by VnExpress/Luu Quy Network provider VNPT said it rerouted traffic through available connections immediately after the problems emerged to make the best use of its remaining capacity. But Internet access would "be affected to some extent" during peak hours, it said. Users might experience slower connections when browsing websites, streaming videos, or playing games hosted on overseas servers, though Internet services generally remain stable because of backup infrastructure, it said. The company described the incident as a force majeure event that affects all Internet service providers in Vietnam. A Viettel spokesperson told VnExpress that the company has been affected by the problems with the IA and AAE-1 cables. Its AAE-1 connection has been completely disrupted, sharply reducing the company's international capacity though its backup systems have not recorded any overload. To compensate for the lost capacity, Viettel added 800 Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable Wednesday. It is also adding 300 Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway, with the additional capacity expected to be available by Aug. 31. It has also rerouted some international traffic through a terrestrial cable running via Laos to Singapore and plans to add another 1.5 Tbps of capacity on that route by the end of the month. It said it could increase capacity on its Asia Direct Cable (ADC) to 50 Tbps if needed to "handle all international Internet traffic." The ADC, which was installed in 2025, links Vietnam with three major Asian connectivity hubs Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan. Vietnam is linked by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems, AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC and SJC2, the last two being the newest. The systems have suffered some 10 incidents a year since 2022. Repairs to undersea cables typically take several months to half a year and can sometimes take as long as a year. To reduce its dependence on undersea cables, Vietnam launched its first VSTN terrestrial fiber-optic cable in 2025 and has also approved trials of satellite Internet services. Capacity loss: Before reports of the fourth fault emerged, Tuổi Trẻ News reported on August 27 that problems affecting SJC2, AAE-1 and AAG had reduced Vietnam’s total international internet capacity by about 30%, citing preliminary estimates from several telecom operators. The newspaper said providers had activated contingency measures and were rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Repair status: SJC2 reportedly suffered a failure near Chung Hom Kok in Hong Kong, while AAE-1 experienced a separate connectivity failure. Repair work is also pending or underway on other affected routes, although schedules vary by cable and remain dependent on factors including specialized repair-vessel availability and weather conditions. Timeline uncertainty: Reports differ on when some of the individual failures occurred and on repair schedules, leaving the precise sequence and current status of the outages unclear pending confirmation from cable operators and consortium representatives. The simultaneous problems highlight the vulnerability of Vietnam’s international communications infrastructure even as the country expands its submarine cable capacity. Multiple cable failures can place greater pressure on remaining routes and expose limits in redundancy when repairs cannot be completed quickly. Traffic rerouting: Vietnamese internet providers are redirecting international traffic across unaffected submarine and terrestrial connections to maintain service. The key question is whether those alternative routes can provide sufficient capacity until repairs are completed, particularly during peak periods when users accessing overseas services may experience slower speeds and higher latency. Undersea cable disruptions may affect some Internet services, particularly online gaming, in Vietnam. article.content: 1.3 min read India Plans Faster Subsea Cable Repair Clearances Danish Khan, Moneycontrol August 25, 2026 India’s Department of Telecommunications is developing a single-window portal intended to reduce delays in approvals for submarine cable repairs. The proposed platform would bring agencies involved in the clearance process onto one system, including shipping authorities, the Coast Guard and the Ministry of Home Affairs. Telecom operators are affected by cable faults, but many repair permissions currently sit with other government bodies. The department expects to complete a proposal for the portal in about two months. After that, the plan would move through approvals, procurement, tendering and implementation. An information technology agency under the Centre for Development of Telematics is expected to participate, with March 2027 identified as a tentative implementation target. DoT is also discussing the development of domestic repair capability with industry and the Directorate General of Shipping. India does not currently have a dedicated submarine cable repair vessel and relies on foreign resources, which can increase costs and extend restoration times when suitable vessels are unavailable or operating elsewhere. Building a domestic ecosystem would require investment in a specialized vessel and supporting infrastructure. The initiative comes as international cable routes face operational and geopolitical risks. Multiple Red Sea cable faults in 2024 affected systems between Asia and Europe, although Indian operators largely mitigated the impact by rerouting traffic. A faster domestic clearance process and locally based repair resources could reduce the time needed to respond when future faults affect cables serving India. article.content: Saturday, August 29, 2026 Sign in Hello, Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Vietnam News Ho Chi Minh City Travel Economy Education Expat Life World Video Photo Vietnam News Thursday, August 27, 2026, 14:49 GMT+7 Vietnam’s international Internet connection affected by faults on three undersea cables Three undersea cable systems serving Vietnam have encountered problems, cutting the country’s international Internet capacity by an estimated 30 percent and potentially causing slower connections during peak hours. Undersea cable disruptions may affect some Internet services, particularly online gaming, in Vietnam. Photo: Duc Thien / Tuoi Tre The SJC2 and AAE-1 cables recently suffered outages while repairs to the AAG system have yet to be completed, according to domestic telecom operators and international cable management units. AAE-1, which links Vietnam with Hong Kong and Singapore, experienced an incident at 6:22 pm on Tuesday. Repair work is expected to begin in late September, depending on the availability of specialized vessels and weather conditions at sea. Starlink satellite Internet launches in Vietnam Vietnam’s Internet infrastructure ready to power low-altitude economy With AAG still under repair following an earlier fault, three of Vietnam’s major international undersea cable systems are now affected. According to preliminary estimates from several telecom operators, the outages have reduced Vietnam’s total international Internet capacity by about 30 percent. Internet service providers have activated contingency measures, rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Vietnam’s telecommunications provider VNPT said it had balanced and redirected traffic across alternative routes to optimize available capacity, helping keep its network generally stable. However, users may experience slower speeds and higher latency during peak hours when accessing overseas-hosted services, including websites, high-definition video streaming, and online games. Some operators said the impact on customers remained limited thanks to backup capacity across multiple independent routes. Vietnam currently relies mainly on six undersea cable systems for international Internet connectivity: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2. SJC2 spans about 10,500 kilometers across the Asia-Pacific region, with an initial investment of US$439 million and a designed capacity of up to 126 Tbps. original_text: Rostelecom says it has completed repairs to the Kamchatka-Sakhalin submarine fiber line and restored full telecommunications service on August 14, 2026. The work took place in the Ust-Bolsheretsky district under difficult marine and weather conditions. The project focused on improving the cable's shore-end route in the shallow coastal waters of the Sea of Okhotsk. Divers exposed the existing cable at depths of up to five meters, roughly one hundred fifty meters from shore, cut it on the seabed and transferred a section to a pontoon. Technicians then spliced in about four hundred meters of new cable installed from land by horizontal directional drilling. Divers subsequently buried the cable in the seabed. Onshore crews installed and buried another one hundred fifty meters of new cable and added a shore joint. Rostelecom said the revised route follows a safer coastal alignment intended to improve reliability and reduce the risk of future damage.

article.content: 1.2 min read Rostelecom Restores Kamchatka-Sakhalin Cable Rostelecom, Press Release August 14, 2026 Rostelecom says it has completed repairs to the Kamchatka-Sakhalin submarine fiber line and restored full telecommunications service on August 14, 2026. The work took place in the Ust-Bolsheretsky district under difficult marine and weather conditions. The project focused on improving the cable's shore-end route in the shallow coastal waters of the Sea of Okhotsk. Divers exposed the existing cable at depths of up to five meters, roughly one hundred fifty meters from shore, cut it on the seabed and transferred a section to a pontoon. Technicians then spliced in about four hundred meters of new cable installed from land by horizontal directional drilling. Divers subsequently buried the cable in the seabed. Onshore crews installed and buried another one hundred fifty meters of new cable and added a shore joint. Rostelecom said the revised route follows a safer coastal alignment intended to improve reliability and reduce the risk of future damage. Specialists from BULAT, including divers, supported the preventative work. The project focused on improving the cable's shore-end route in the shallow coastal waters of the Sea of Okhotsk. Divers exposed the existing cable at depths of up to five meters, roughly one hundred fifty meters from shore, cut it on the seabed and transferred a section to a pontoon. Technicians then spliced in about four hundred meters of new cable installed from land by horizontal directional drilling. Divers subsequently buried the cable in the seabed. Onshore crews installed and buried another one hundred fifty meters of new cable and added a shore joint. Rostelecom said the revised route follows a safer coastal alignment intended to improve reliability and reduce the risk of future damage. Specialists from BULAT, including divers, supported the preventative work. Full service has resumed in Kamchatka, parts of Chukotka and Severo-Kurilsk on Sakhalin, with online services operating without speed restrictions. article.content: JEAN-SEBASTIEN EVRARD/Stringer/Getty Earlier this week, Bevan Slattery, the chief executive of subsea cable company SubCo, announced that two cables had experienced faults over the weekend. He deemed it a “concerning development” because these “submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation”. Slattery called on federal police to investigate the issue urgently . The subsea cable damage occurred within the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone , an area specifically designed to keep these cables safe. However, this safe zone extends over 100 kilometers offshore with the cables on the seabed, making them difficult to monitor and access. But there is a way Australia can practically safeguard these cables. Connecting us to the rest of the world Australia is connected to the global internet by fewer than two dozen undersea fibre optic cables, which carry more than 95% of our international internet traffic. Each cable has multiple strands of optical fibre – structured glass about an eighth of a millimetre across – and can carry more than 20 terabits per second. In other words, two of these fibres could carry all of the National Broadband Network’s data . The Indigo West and Indigo Central cables that were affected connect Perth to Sydney, and Perth to Jakarta and Singapore. These are part of a web of fibre optic cables that connect Australia to the world. Australia’s access to the global internet depends on a surprisingly small number of undersea cables – just 22 are connected or currently being built . Satellites are valuable for connecting remote areas, but they cannot yet carry anything like the enormous amount of data that travels through these cables. This map shows the approximate location of international submarine cables presently landing in Australia. Australian Communications and Media Authority What could have caused the damage? Slattery called the issues a “ shunt fault ”. This is where the electrical part of the cable is damaged, degrading performance or stopping the cable from working entirely. Subsea optical cables are able to span thousands of kilometres due to the use of optical amplifiers which boost the signal every 50 to 100 kilometres. These optical amplifiers need electrical power to run, and so high-voltage direct current power is transmitted through metal wires alongside the glass optical fibres. There can be multiple causes of shunt faults that short out this power supply. There is increasing concern about deliberate interference. But most often these faults are accidental , caused by anchors or trawler nets dragging along the seafloor . Slattery said we “will not know the root cause” of the fault “until the cable is recovered during repair”. But how can we more effectively monitor these cables? Home-grown tech to keep us connected to the world Distributed acoustic sensing is a laser technology that can sense vibrations travelling across fibre optic cables. It is an evolving technology only recently adopted by fibre optic communications companies for monitoring their infrastructure. You can think of this technology a bit like shouting “coo-ee”: listening for the echoes can tell you something about what they reflected off. Similarly, distributed acoustic sensing measures light “echoing” off small changes along the length of a fibre. Crucially, it can sense the environment around the fibre to tell us things about vessel activity, seabed disturbances, and other physical interactions near the cable. The technology can also be used to map the structure of the soil and rock around the fibre, or to monitor and provide early warning of earthquakes and tsunamis. Slattery said that if distributed acoustic sensing had been installed on the affected cables, it would have been possible to identify the vessel responsible for the fault almost instantly. He also said that because the technology is installed on nearby unaffected cables in the same area, “we can confirm no seabed activity around or near” those other cables. Working towards more resilient national infrastructure Distributed acoustic sensing can provide both environmental monitoring of the world around us and a way to safeguard key national infrastructure. Our team’s work has also shown that this evolving technology and high speed data can simultaneously work right next to each other in the same fibre . This is important as telcos have stringent requirements on keeping data flowing through these cables, with heavy penalties for non-compliance. We think we can help get more distributed acoustic sensing into our fibres in two ways: by demonstrating it can live side-by-side in modern optical communications systems with data, and by leveraging optical microcomb technologies to make the technology smaller, better, and perhaps cheaper. Our research is showing that the existing fibres that connect Australia to the rest of the world could carry significantly more data than they are currently. They could also reveal new insights about the world around us. By making this technology affordable and deployable, we will make Australia’s future communications networks not only faster, but safer and more resilient. title: Two subsea cables off Perth suffer ‘concerning’ damage. Lasers could help protect them

original_text: Subco has reported concurrent faults affecting two cables in the Perth area and called for an investigation while the operator prepares a physical inspection. The Maritime Executive reported that the outages occurred in a government-designated cable protection zone and involved two Subco systems in the same area. The cause of the faults has not been established. Subco says the affected cables do not have automatic diagnostic systems, so the operator will need to arrange a physical inspection before it can determine the mechanism of damage. That limitation is important: any explanation for the faults remains unconfirmed until the inspection is complete. The report noted the track of a vessel that crossed the cable zone around the time of the outages, but it also quoted Subco's chief executive saying the activity could be coincidental.

article.content: JEAN-SEBASTIEN EVRARD/Stringer/Getty Earlier this week, Bevan Slattery, the chief executive of subsea cable company SubCo, announced that two cables had experienced faults over the weekend. He deemed it a “concerning development” because these “submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation”. Slattery called on federal police to investigate the issue urgently . The subsea cable damage occurred within the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone , an area specifically designed to keep these cables safe. However, this safe zone extends over 100 kilometers offshore with the cables on the seabed, making them difficult to monitor and access. But there is a way Australia can practically safeguard these cables. Connecting us to the rest of the world Australia is connected to the global internet by fewer than two dozen undersea fibre optic cables, which carry more than 95% of our international internet traffic. Each cable has multiple strands of optical fibre – structured glass about an eighth of a millimetre across – and can carry more than 20 terabits per second. In other words, two of these fibres could carry all of the National Broadband Network’s data . The Indigo West and Indigo Central cables that were affected connect Perth to Sydney, and Perth to Jakarta and Singapore. These are part of a web of fibre optic cables that connect Australia to the world. Australia’s access to the global internet depends on a surprisingly small number of undersea cables – just 22 are connected or currently being built . Satellites are valuable for connecting remote areas, but they cannot yet carry anything like the enormous amount of data that travels through these cables. This map shows the approximate location of international submarine cables presently landing in Australia. Australian Communications and Media Authority What could have caused the damage? Slattery called the issues a “ shunt fault ”. This is where the electrical part of the cable is damaged, degrading performance or stopping the cable from working entirely. Subsea optical cables are able to span thousands of kilometres due to the use of optical amplifiers which boost the signal every 50 to 100 kilometres. These optical amplifiers need electrical power to run, and so high-voltage direct current power is transmitted through metal wires alongside the glass optical fibres. There can be multiple causes of shunt faults that short out this power supply. There is increasing concern about deliberate interference. But most often these faults are accidental , caused by anchors or trawler nets dragging along the seafloor . Slattery said we “will not know the root cause” of the fault “until the cable is recovered during repair”. But how can we more effectively monitor these cables? Home-grown tech to keep us connected to the world Distributed acoustic sensing is a laser technology that can sense vibrations travelling across fibre optic cables. It is an evolving technology only recently adopted by fibre optic communications companies for monitoring their infrastructure. You can think of this technology a bit like shouting “coo-ee”: listening for the echoes can tell you something about what they reflected off. Similarly, distributed acoustic sensing measures light “echoing” off small changes along the length of a fibre. Crucially, it can sense the environment around the fibre to tell us things about vessel activity, seabed disturbances, and other physical interactions near the cable. The technology can also be used to map the structure of the soil and rock around the fibre, or to monitor and provide early warning of earthquakes and tsunamis. Slattery said that if distributed acoustic sensing had been installed on the affected cables, it would have been possible to identify the vessel responsible for the fault almost instantly. He also said that because the technology is installed on nearby unaffected cables in the same area, “we can confirm no seabed activity around or near” those other cables. Working towards more resilient national infrastructure Distributed acoustic sensing can provide both environmental monitoring of the world around us and a way to safeguard key national infrastructure. Our team’s work has also shown that this evolving technology and high speed data can simultaneously work right next to each other in the same fibre . This is important as telcos have stringent requirements on keeping data flowing through these cables, with heavy penalties for non-compliance. We think we can help get more distributed acoustic sensing into our fibres in two ways: by demonstrating it can live side-by-side in modern optical communications systems with data, and by leveraging optical microcomb technologies to make the technology smaller, better, and perhaps cheaper. Our research is showing that the existing fibres that connect Australia to the rest of the world could carry significantly more data than they are currently. They could also reveal new insights about the world around us. By making this technology affordable and deployable, we will make Australia’s future communications networks not only faster, but safer and more resilient. article.content: 1.2 min read Kamchatka Prepares for Subsea Cable Repairs The Moscow Times Staff, The Moscow Times August 10, 2026 Kamchatka authorities say maintenance on an undersea fiber-optic cable will cause a near-total internet interruption across Russia’s Far Eastern peninsula for as long as four days. The work is scheduled to begin at midnight local time on Wednesday and will be carried out by state telecommunications provider Rostelecom. The regional government said timing remains weather-dependent. Mobile and home internet services are expected to be unavailable during the maintenance window, affecting messaging apps, social platforms and other online services. Officials said conventional voice calls, SMS, television broadcasts and emergency services should continue operating. Hospitals, fuel stations, supermarkets, automated teller machines and other critical infrastructure are expected to switch to satellite backup connections while the main fiber link is offline. The government advised Kamchatka’s roughly 280,000 residents to prepare before the outage by obtaining cash and arranging offline resources. The announcement frames the disruption as planned maintenance rather than an unexpected cable fault. The work had previously been scheduled for September 2025 but was postponed, according to The Moscow Times. The latest notice establishes a new operational window and gives the region advance warning, though it does not identify the precise cable section, describe the technical repair scope or provide a guaranteed restoration time. Service duration will depend on repair progress and weather conditions. The regional government said timing remains weather-dependent. Mobile and home internet services are expected to be unavailable during the maintenance window, affecting messaging apps, social platforms and other online services. Officials said conventional voice calls, SMS, television broadcasts and emergency services should continue operating. Hospitals, fuel stations, supermarkets, automated teller machines and other critical infrastructure are expected to switch to satellite backup connections while the main fiber link is offline. The government advised Kamchatka’s roughly 280,000 residents to prepare before the outage by obtaining cash and arranging offline resources. The announcement frames the disruption as planned maintenance rather than an unexpected cable fault. The work had previously been scheduled for September 2025 but was postponed, according to The Moscow Times. The latest notice establishes a new operational window and gives the region advance warning, though it does not identify the precise cable section, describe the technical repair scope or provide a guaranteed restoration time. Service duration will depend on repair progress and weather conditions. Shunt faults in undersea cables refer to a condition where the outer insulating layers of the line become damaged exposing the interior components to sea water and are commonly attributed to ships' anchors and fishing activity.
original_text_zh: SUBCO在其连接新加坡和悉尼并在珀斯设有登陆点的Indigo West和Indigo Central海底电缆系统中检测到“旁路故障”。海底电缆的旁路故障指的是电缆外部绝缘层受损，导致内部组件暴露于海水中的情况，这通常归因于船只锚和捕鱼活动。

article.content: Home News Technology Telco/ISP AFP assessing report in connection with Perth cable faults By Andrew Colley Aug 11 2026 6:42AM Singapore-Perth link goes dark after shunt faults detected. The Australian Federal Police is assessing a report of a potential crime after the owner of two undersea cables laid in protection zones near Perth revealed faults commonly attributed to ship activity. Bevan Slattery, co-chief and founder of SUBCO, which owns the two Indigo cable systems, confirmed to iTnews that the company reported the incidents to the AFP which, he said, occurred near each other and at a similar time. Slattery first raised the alarm about the incidents in a post on LinkedIn on the weekend, shortly after SUBCO detected “shunt faults” on its Indigo West and Indigo Central cable systems, which together connect Singapore and Sydney with a landing at Perth in-between. Shunt faults in undersea cables refer to a condition where the outer insulating layers of the line become damaged exposing the interior components to sea water and are commonly attributed to ships' anchors and fishing activity. A spokesperson for the AFP told iTnews that the agency was looking into the incident but stopped short of saying it is actively investigating it as a crime. “The AFP has received a report of crime in relation to this matter. This report is currently being assessed based on the information provided. Further comment will be made at an appropriate time,” the spokesperson said. In the LinkedIn post, Slattery pointed to a ship tracking chart showing what he described as “suspicious/coincidental” vessel activity in the area. However, he stopped short of declaring that the cables had been deliberately damaged. “This could be a coincidence or an external aggression event,” Slattery wrote, explaining that the cause of the fault would have been known instantly had the cables been monitored using FibreSense, an advanced detection system used on some of SUBCO’s other undersea cables. “Indigo West and Central do not have FiberSense installed and, unfortunately, the consortium will not know the root cause until the cable is recovered during repair,” he wrote. Nevertheless, Slattery said that it was still important that authorities investigate as it may be the second time such an incident has occurred in a cable protection zone. “This maybe a coincidence, but it’s important for the Australian Federal Police to investigate the issue urgently,” Slattery wrote. Regional internet provider AusInternet, which uses the Indigo West cable, has been advising of an outage on the link on its website since Saturday evening, saying that it has been routing traffic around the apparent break. Early yesterday it was advising customers that the earliest fix to the cable was expected August 26. “The Indigo team has engaged their marine maintenance operator for vessel allocation and planning of the repairs. ETA is on August 26 2026. All timelines remain subject to clearance, logistics arrangement and weather conditions,” it advised. Slattery said that SUBCO would be following up its report to the AFP with more information soon. Add iTnews as your trusted source Got a news tip for our journalists? article.content: 1.3 min read Four Cable Faults Disrupt Vietnam International Traffic Publication Staff, VOV.VN August 28, 2026 Four of Vietnam’s eight international submarine cable systems are facing technical problems, creating pressure on overseas internet connectivity, according to VOV. The affected routes are SJC2, AAE-1, AAG and Intra-Asia, or IA. The latest status makes IA the fourth system currently listed as impaired. Cable operators said SJC2 and AAE-1 developed faults nearly at the same time on August 25, 2026. AAG was already affected by an unresolved issue, while IA has also been hit. Repair activity for IA is expected to start in early September, but no repair timetable has been released for SJC2, AAE-1 or AAG. SJC2 and AAE-1 are significant links for Vietnam’s international internet capacity. SJC2 is designed for up to 126 Tbps and includes investment from VNPT, with a landing point in Quy Nhon. AAE-1 has about 40 Tbps of design capacity and extends from Asia toward networks in the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Viettel is the cable’s only partner in Vietnam and manages the local landing facilities. AAG connects Southeast Asia with the United States and has been operating for many years. Users may see localized slowdowns at busy times when accessing overseas social media, streaming platforms and online games. Services and websites hosted inside Vietnam are not expected to be affected. Internet providers in Vietnam have responded with contingency steps, including traffic rerouting and load balancing through working submarine systems and land-based networks. Capacity loss: Before reports of the fourth fault emerged, Tuổi Trẻ News reported on August 27 that problems affecting SJC2, AAE-1 and AAG had reduced Vietnam’s total international internet capacity by about 30%, citing preliminary estimates from several telecom operators. The newspaper said providers had activated contingency measures and were rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Repair status: SJC2 reportedly suffered a failure near Chung Hom Kok in Hong Kong, while AAE-1 experienced a separate connectivity failure. Repair work is also pending or underway on other affected routes, although schedules vary by cable and remain dependent on factors including specialized repair-vessel availability and weather conditions. Timeline uncertainty: Reports differ on when some of the individual failures occurred and on repair schedules, leaving the precise sequence and current status of the outages unclear pending confirmation from cable operators and consortium representatives. The simultaneous problems highlight the vulnerability of Vietnam’s international communications infrastructure even as the country expands its submarine cable capacity. Multiple cable failures can place greater pressure on remaining routes and expose limits in redundancy when repairs cannot be completed quickly. Traffic rerouting: Vietnamese internet providers are redirecting international traffic across unaffected submarine and terrestrial connections to maintain service. The key question is whether those alternative routes can provide sufficient capacity until repairs are completed, particularly during peak periods when users accessing overseas services may experience slower speeds and higher latency. Capacity loss: Before reports of the fourth fault emerged, Tuổi Trẻ News reported on August 27 that problems affecting SJC2, AAE-1 and AAG had reduced Vietnam’s total international internet capacity by about 30%, citing preliminary estimates from several telecom operators. The newspaper said providers had activated contingency measures and were rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Repair status: SJC2 reportedly suffered a failure near Chung Hom Kok in Hong Kong, while AAE-1 experienced a separate connectivity failure. Repair work is also pending or underway on other affected routes, although schedules vary by cable and remain dependent on factors including specialized repair-vessel availability and weather conditions. Timeline uncertainty: Reports differ on when some of the individual failures occurred and on repair schedules, leaving the precise sequence and current status of the outages unclear pending confirmation from cable operators and consortium representatives. The simultaneous problems highlight the vulnerability of Vietnam’s international communications infrastructure even as the country expands its submarine cable capacity. Multiple cable failures can place greater pressure on remaining routes and expose limits in redundancy when repairs cannot be completed quickly. Traffic rerouting: Vietnamese internet providers are redirecting international traffic across unaffected submarine and terrestrial connections to maintain service. The key question is whether those alternative routes can provide sufficient capacity until repairs are completed, particularly during peak periods when users accessing overseas services may experience slower speeds and higher latency. article.content: 2.2 min read Introducing Our Next-Generation Cable Maintenance Vessel Megan Annals, Global Marine July 27, 2026 Global Marine Group is pleased to announce the signing of a contract for the construction of a new, purpose-built cable maintenance vessel. The cable ship will be built at Colombo Dockyard in Sri Lanka, with scheduled delivery in Q4 2029. Designed specifically for fibre optic submarine cable repair operations, this new build represents a significant investment in the future of our fleet and the markets we serve. Based on a proven next generation vessel design, the new build will deliver enhanced operational performance while setting new standards in efficiency and sustainability. It marks the first step in a planned and phased renewal of our fleet, introducing a modern, hybrid-powered platform optimised for subsea cable maintenance. Built for Performance and Sustainability The new vessel has been engineered with a strong focus on station-keeping capability and reduced fuel consumption. Key features include: Hybrid power generation, combining generators and battery systems to enhance operational efficiency and resilience Optimised fuel consumption, using advanced engine configurations to match power output to operating conditions Azimuth thruster technology, delivering maximum propulsion efficiency and manoeuvrability A hydrodynamically optimised hull, improving transit efficiency and performance in challenging sea states Shore power connectivity, enabling reduced emissions during standby periods Advanced emissions reduction systems, supporting compliance with CLEANSHIP requirements and future regulatory standards Together, these capabilities deliver meaningful reductions in CO 2 and NOx emissions, alongside improved operational reliability. Simon Hibberd, Chief Executive Officer, Global Marine Group, said: “This new build is about investing ahead of demand. It ensures Global Marine has the capability, capacity, and efficiency required to support the next generation of subsea cable networks while reinforcing our position as the market-leading provider of maintenance services worldwide. We are delighted to be partnering with Colombo Dockyard on this important project and look forward to welcoming the vessel into service in 2029.” Supporting Long-Term Growth This new build, alongside the recent acquisition of CS Clipper, represents a significant renewal of our operational fleet. It strengthens our ability to support long-term maintenance contracts with the world’s leading cable owners, while positioning us to capitalise on the growing demand in the subsea cable market. As the industry enters a phase of structural expansion and tighter environmental regulation, investing in modern, fuel-efficient vessels ensures we remain competitive, resilient, and ready to meet future challenges. Designed for the Future With cutting-edge hydrodynamic design and a specification tailored to our exact operational requirements, this vessel will be built for long-term performance, delivering strong sea-keeping capabilities and full lifecycle value. In a market with increasing demand, this investment puts us in a strong position to win and retain work in the years ahead. original_text: Conatel: Venezuela Recupera el 100% de Conectividad Internacional Tras Concluir la Reparación del Cable Submarino. Venezuela’s National Telecommunications Commission, Conatel, has announced the full restoration of the country’s international connectivity after the Wave Sentinel completed repairs to a damaged Cirion subsea cable.
original_text_zh: 委内瑞拉国家电信委员会Conatel宣布，在Wave Sentinel完成对受损的Cirion海底电缆的修复后，该国国际连接已完全恢复。

article.content: 1.3 min read Conatel: Venezuela Recupera el 100% de Conectividad Internacional Tras Concluir la Reparación del Cable Submarino Barbara Rodríguez, FMUC 104.5 – Universidad de Carabobo July 24, 2026 Venezuela’s National Telecommunications Commission, Conatel, has announced the full restoration of the country’s international connectivity after the Wave Sentinel completed repairs to a damaged Cirion subsea cable. Conatel said definitive link tests showed the network had returned to its original design specifications and performance standards. The restored infrastructure is once again carrying the international capacity required by Venezuela’s digital ecosystem, moving the incident from an active repair operation to a completed restoration. The regulator attributed the accelerated response to coordination among government authorities, Conatel and the private sector. It said permitting and logistical work that can take an average of 45 days was completed within a 14-day repair window. The Wave Sentinel’s crew and engineering teams then performed the reconnection and final testing at sea. Conatel also said it maintained technical supervision throughout the maritime work. That oversight followed the earlier start of Cirion’s Venezuela cable repair and supported each phase of the operation through the final reconnection. According to the announcement, the repaired cable belongs to a regional infrastructure footprint covering more than one hundred five thousand kilometers of fiber and 18 cable landing stations. The network connects to the regional Tier-1 backbone identified as AS3356. With testing complete and capacity restored, Conatel says the system is again operating at its intended performance level. article.content: 2.2 min read Introducing Our Next-Generation Cable Maintenance Vessel Megan Annals, Global Marine July 27, 2026 Global Marine Group is pleased to announce the signing of a contract for the construction of a new, purpose-built cable maintenance vessel. The cable ship will be built at Colombo Dockyard in Sri Lanka, with scheduled delivery in Q4 2029. Designed specifically for fibre optic submarine cable repair operations, this new build represents a significant investment in the future of our fleet and the markets we serve. Based on a proven next generation vessel design, the new build will deliver enhanced operational performance while setting new standards in efficiency and sustainability. It marks the first step in a planned and phased renewal of our fleet, introducing a modern, hybrid-powered platform optimised for subsea cable maintenance. Built for Performance and Sustainability The new vessel has been engineered with a strong focus on station-keeping capability and reduced fuel consumption. Key features include: Hybrid power generation, combining generators and battery systems to enhance operational efficiency and resilience Optimised fuel consumption, using advanced engine configurations to match power output to operating conditions Azimuth thruster technology, delivering maximum propulsion efficiency and manoeuvrability A hydrodynamically optimised hull, improving transit efficiency and performance in challenging sea states Shore power connectivity, enabling reduced emissions during standby periods Advanced emissions reduction systems, supporting compliance with CLEANSHIP requirements and future regulatory standards Together, these capabilities deliver meaningful reductions in CO 2 and NOx emissions, alongside improved operational reliability. Simon Hibberd, Chief Executive Officer, Global Marine Group, said: “This new build is about investing ahead of demand. It ensures Global Marine has the capability, capacity, and efficiency required to support the next generation of subsea cable networks while reinforcing our position as the market-leading provider of maintenance services worldwide. We are delighted to be partnering with Colombo Dockyard on this important project and look forward to welcoming the vessel into service in 2029.” Supporting Long-Term Growth This new build, alongside the recent acquisition of CS Clipper, represents a significant renewal of our operational fleet. It strengthens our ability to support long-term maintenance contracts with the world’s leading cable owners, while positioning us to capitalise on the growing demand in the subsea cable market. As the industry enters a phase of structural expansion and tighter environmental regulation, investing in modern, fuel-efficient vessels ensures we remain competitive, resilient, and ready to meet future challenges. Designed for the Future With cutting-edge hydrodynamic design and a specification tailored to our exact operational requirements, this vessel will be built for long-term performance, delivering strong sea-keeping capabilities and full lifecycle value. In a market with increasing demand, this investment puts us in a strong position to win and retain work in the years ahead. original_text: The Wave Sentinel Begins Repair Work on the Cirion Subsea Cable in Venezuela Publication Staff, Cirion Technologies July 19, 2026 Cirion Technologies says repair work has begun on the affected subsea cable in Venezuelan waters after the Wave Sentinel completed its entry procedures and reached the work area. The cable-repair vessel is now supporting technical operations at the reported damage point. An underwater robot was sent down to the cut location and located both ends of the broken cable. Specialized teams have started integrity and connectivity tests, with the findings expected to determine the next immediate repair actions. Cirion said future updates will describe the condition of the cable following the earthquake and document progress toward restoration.
original_text_zh: 《The Wave Sentinel开始修复委内瑞拉的Cirion海底电缆》发布人员，Cirion Technologies，2026年7月19日 - Cirion Technologies表示，在Wave Sentinel完成入境程序并到达工作区域后，已开始对委内瑞拉水域受影响的电缆进行修复工作。修复船现在正在报告的损坏点技术支持操作。水下机器人已被派往切断位置并找到了断裂电缆的两端。专业团队已开始进行完整性和连通性测试，预计测试结果将决定接下来的修复行动。Cirion表示，未来更新将描述地震后电缆的状况并记录恢复进展。

article.content: 1.3 min read The Wave Sentinel Begins Repair Work on the Cirion Subsea Cable in Venezuela Publication Staff, Cirion Technologies July 19, 2026 Cirion Technologies says repair work has begun on the affected subsea cable in Venezuelan waters after the Wave Sentinel completed its entry procedures and reached the work area. The cable-repair vessel is now supporting technical operations at the reported damage point. An underwater robot was sent down to the cut location and located both ends of the broken cable. Specialized teams have started integrity and connectivity tests, with the findings expected to determine the next immediate repair actions. Cirion said future updates will describe the condition of the cable following the earthquake and document progress toward restoration. The offshore work follows several preparatory milestones. Cirion previously reported that it had stabilized the network, progressively expanded available capacity, handled regulatory requirements, and mobilized the Wave Sentinel to Venezuela. With the vessel now on site, the response has moved from contingency preparation to direct inspection and repair activity on the subsea infrastructure. Cirion emphasized that it will base subsequent notices on confirmed technical information and work actually completed. That approach means the current development is an inspection-and-testing milestone rather than confirmation that the repair itself has finished. The company operates terrestrial and subsea fiber infrastructure across Latin America, alongside interconnection, cloud-connectivity, colocation, and other digital services. The results of the ongoing cable tests should provide the clearest indication of the damage condition, the repair method required, and the remaining path to restored connectivity. article.content: 1.5 min read Chinese Barge Captain Not Prosecuted Over Dongyin Subsea Cable Damage By Focus Taiwan July 15, 2026 Taipei, July 15 (CNA) The Lienchiang District Prosecutors Office announced Wednesday that it will not prosecute the captain of a Chinese-flagged work barge, which damaged a subsea cable off Dongyin Island on March 30, citing insufficient evidence. According to a statement from the prosecutors' office, the incident occurred on March 30, when captain Ho (何) of the Hai Hong Gong 66 was carrying out a towing operation to remove the stranded Chinese fishing vessel Min Lian Yu 63896. Prosecutors stated that a fragment of the stranded fishing vessel struck and damaged the core wire of the Dongyin-Beigan section of Taiwan-Matsu Subsea Cable No. 3, which is owned and operated by Chunghwa Telecom. During questioning, Ho denied intentionally damaging the cable, saying he had contacted Chunghwa Telecom personnel before beginning the operation to confirm where the vessel could safely anchor. Ho said there were no abnormalities during the operation and he immediately halted work after being notified that the cable had been damaged. The prosecutors' statement said after Min Lian Yu 63896 ran aground, its owner initially proposed a salvage plan that included a preliminary underwater survey. However, because of national security concerns, the owner later submitted a revised plan removing the underwater inspection, which was approved by the relevant Taiwanese authorities. Because no underwater survey was conducted before the operation and underwater work was not permitted, those involved could not determine the conditions around the stranded vessel or the exact location of the subsea cable. As a result, it was decided that Chunghwa Telecom personnel would identify a safe anchoring location that avoided the cable before the work barge dropped anchor, according to the statement. original_text_zh: 海底电缆故障或导致网络间歇性中断：PTA 卡尔贝·阿里 发布于2026年7月2日 伊斯兰堡：巴基斯坦电信管理局（PTA）周四表示，正密切监控由SEA-ME-WE 5（SMW5）国际海底电缆系统故障引发的网络中断问题，该故障可能导致服务质量与连接性出现间歇性下降。

article.content: PTA says submarine cable fault resolved, internet services back to normal News Desk Published July 3, 2026 0 A man explores social media on a computer at an internet club in Islamabad on August 11, 2016. — Reuters/File Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x comments Join our Whatsapp Channel Add Dawn as a trusted source The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) announced on Friday that internet services in the country were back to normal after issues with the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system were resolved. In a statement, the authority said that the fault in the cable system, which had led to widespread connectivity issues in the country on Thursday night, had been resolved, adding that internet traffic had returned to normal. It said Transworld Associates’ (TWA) international transit capacity has been restored. According to its website, TWA is the only private-sector operator with exclusive ownership of submarine fibre-optic cable systems. Subsequently, internet service provider Nayatel said that “international traffic has returned to normal”. “Our teams continue to closely monitor the network to ensure service stability,” it said. On Thursday night, the PTA had said that a technical fault along the SMW5 route was affecting data traffic. It had said that “some internet users may experience intermittent degradation in service quality and connectivity as a result of the fault.” In November, a new submarine internet cable — the South-East Asia–Middle East–Western Europe 6 (SEA-ME-WE 6) — landed in Pakistan. The cable has a total capacity of over 100 terabits per second and it will provide “one of the lowest-latency routes between Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Western Europe”, the information technology ministry said. It added that Pakistan has been allocated a total of 13.2tbps. The ministry elaborated that SEA-ME-WE 6 featured “more fibre pairs and more than double the capacity” of previous SEA-ME-WE systems, enhancing resilience and diversification across high-traffic Asia-Europe routes through trans-Egypt geo-diversified crossings and landing points.

It added that Pakistan has been allocated a total of 13.2tbps. The ministry elaborated that SEA-ME-WE 6 features “more fibre pairs and more than double the capacity” of previous SEA-ME-WE systems, enhancing resilience and diversification across high-traffic Asia-Europe routes through trans-Egypt geo-diversified crossings and landing points.

article.content: 1.3 min read Finland to Try Two Sailors Over Baltic Sea Submarine Cable Damage By Alberto Payo, Escudo Digital June 18, 2026 Finland has filed charges against the captain and the navigation officer of a cargo ship accused of damaging underwater telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea during last New Year's Eve, according to the country's prosecutor's office. According to the investigation, the ship—named Fitburg—allegedly caused the breakage of several cables after dragging its anchor over a long stretch of the seabed (at least 130 km) . The incident affected critical underwater communication infrastructures in the region. Finnish authorities intercepted the vessel after detecting the damages and proceeded to detain two crew members, who now face charges for the incidents. The prosecution claims that the captain and the first mate caused breaks in two underwater telecommunications cables and attempted to damage eight additional underwater connections . The defendants deny committing the offenses and argue that Finland does not have jurisdiction to judge the case , as the incident allegedly occurred outside its territorial waters. The decision on the court's jurisdiction and the trial date will fall to the Helsinki district court. Not the first time The case is part of a series of recent incidents that have affected underwater infrastructures in the Baltic Sea, a context in which the possibility of sabotage was initially considered. The repeated incidents raised suspicions of possible acts linked to Russia . In response, NATO reinforced surveillance of the area with frigates, maritime patrol aircraft, and naval drones. article.content: 1.3 min read Finland to Try Two Sailors Over Baltic Sea Submarine Cable Damage By Alberto Payo, Escudo Digital June 18, 2026 Finland has filed charges against the captain and the navigation officer of a cargo ship accused of damaging underwater telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea during last New Year's Eve, according to the country's prosecutor's office. According to the investigation, the ship—named Fitburg—allegedly caused the breakage of several cables after dragging its anchor over a long stretch of the seabed (at least 130 km) . The incident affected critical underwater communication infrastructures in the region. Finnish authorities intercepted the vessel after detecting the damages and proceeded to detain two crew members, who now face charges for the incidents. The prosecution claims that the captain and the first mate caused breaks in two underwater telecommunications cables and attempted to damage eight additional underwater connections . The defendants deny committing the offenses and argue that Finland does not have jurisdiction to judge the case , as the incident allegedly occurred outside its territorial waters. The decision on the court's jurisdiction and the trial date will fall to the Helsinki district court. Not the first time The case is part of a series of recent incidents that have affected underwater infrastructures in the Baltic Sea, a context in which the possibility of sabotage was initially considered. The repeated incidents raised suspicions of possible acts linked to Russia . In response, NATO reinforced surveillance of the area with frigates, maritime patrol aircraft, and naval drones. article.content: Taiwan’s undersea cables are an Indo-Pacific crisis test Taiwan’s Undersea Cables Are an Indo-Pacific Crisis Test WRITTEN BY JING GE 12 June 2026 Taiwan’s undersea cables are not only a communications vulnerability; they are also a test of crisis discipline in the Indo-Pacific. In April 2026, poor weather conditions displaced wreckage off the coast of Taiwan’s remote Dongyin Island, severing an undersea cable . While backup microwave communications preserved basic connectivity, the incident revealed a deeper problem: in a Taiwan Strait crisis, a severed cable could be read as an accident, a coercive signal, or the opening move in a larger confrontation. The strategic risk lies not only in the cut itself, but in the ambiguity that follows. This is why Taiwan’s cable vulnerability should not be treated simply as another US-China flashpoint. It is a test of whether the US, Taiwan, and their Indo-Pacific partners can respond to grey-zone pressure without overreacting to every incident as an act of war. The challenge is to make cable coercion less effective while preserving the time and evidence needed to prevent escalation. Ambiguity is the real risk Taiwan’s digital connectivity rests on a relatively limited cable system. It has 25 submarine cables in total: 15 international links connecting Taiwan to Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Singapore, and the US, and 10 domestic inter-island cables linking the main island with Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu. For Taiwan’s outlying island communities, backup connections remain limited. If one break leaves an island offline for days or weeks, political pressure to respond can rise faster than investigators can determine what happened. The main challenge is not simply how to deter China, but how to respond in a way that is firm, evidentiary, and controlled. The right response is not escalation by default, but resilience by design: better evidence, faster repair, clearer rules, and limited backup connectivity. In early 2025, Taiwan experienced several undersea cable disruptions that raised concerns about whether accidents, negligence, or grey-zone activity were responsible. One serious case involved the Trans-Pacific Express cable, a key link connecting Taiwan with Asia and the US. Taiwanese authorities allege that a foreign-registered vessel operated by a Hong Kong company and crewed by Chinese nationals disabled its tracking system before dragging its anchor across the cable. Two further incidents followed: Taiwan’s Coast Guard reported a suspected attempted cable-cutting incident involving a Mongolia-flagged ship, and the Togo-flagged Hongtai 58 was linked to damage to the cable between Taiwan’s main island and Penghu. Determining responsibility for these vessels is challenging because they often operate in ways that complicate their activities: sailing under flags of convenience, changing names or registrations, masking beneficial ownership, switching off tracking systems, or claiming accidental anchoring. While such incidents may remain technical or legal matters in less contested waters, they can quickly take on deeper strategic significance in the Taiwan Strait. Hence, the risk is not only that cables may be cut, but that governments may feel compelled to respond before evidence is conclusive. China’s role makes this problem harder to separate from the region’s wider infrastructure competition. China is not only a military actor in the Taiwan Strait but also an increasingly important player in the Indo-Pacific’s digital and maritime infrastructure. Although Chinese firms such as HMN Technologies and China Unicom operate as commercial providers of digital connectivity and submarine-cable infrastructure, their projects exist within a broader strategic environment in which cable construction, data routes, port access, maritime presence, and political influence increasingly overlap. HMN Technologies has participated in multiple Indo-Pacific undersea cable projects, while Chinese-backed systems such as the Pakistan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE) cable show how cable routes can connect Asia, Africa, and Europe while reducing dependence on Western-controlled jurisdictions. This does not mean every cable fault around Taiwan should be treated as a Chinese operation. Over-attribution would be dangerous. But under-attribution also carries costs. If China or China-linked actors can exploit ambiguity, flags of convenience, and commercial cover to create pressure while avoiding responsibility, then Taiwan’s cable system becomes a grey-zone vulnerability. The real problem is the political space between accident and attack, where coercion can operate before attribution is settled. Evidence, repair, and rules The response should begin with shared attribution rather than automatic escalation. Taiwan, the US, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Australia, and relevant commercial operators should develop a regional monitoring and notification mechanism that creates a shared factual record before political narratives outrun evidence. Such a mechanism would not need to be militarised. It could combine the Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel identification, satellite imagery, maritime patrol records, port data, and cable operator information to determine whether a vessel loitered unusually in a cable zone, disabled its tracking system, changed identity or flag registration, or repeatedly appeared in high-risk areas. The aim should not be instant accusation, but evidence preservation and crisis control. Repair capacity is equally important. Cable disruption becomes more politically dangerous when restoration takes too long. If an outlying island loses connectivity for days or weeks, public pressure will grow, and governments may feel compelled to frame the incident in security terms. But if service can be restored quickly, the incident is more likely to remain within technical, legal, and law-enforcement channels. Repair ships, spare parts, emergency repair agreements, regional repair ports, and cooperation with commercial operators may sound less dramatic than military signalling, but they directly reduce the coercive value of disruption. The faster Taiwan can restore connectivity, the less useful cable cutting becomes as a tool of pressure. A third requirement is bounded accountability. Taiwan has already moved to treat submarine cables as critical infrastructure. In 2025, Taiwan’s Executive Yuan approved draft amendments involving seven laws, including the Telecommunications Management Act, the Electricity Act, the Natural Gas Enterprise Act, the Water Supply Act, the Meteorological Act, the Commercial Port Act, and the Ships Act, to strengthen protection for submarine cables, pipelines, and related infrastructure. Taiwan has also discussed stronger penalties for damaging submarine cables and measures allowing the government to seize related vessels or equipment in cases of illegality. The next step is to connect domestic protection with regional and international standards. In practice, a regional protocol should establish common rules for incident reporting, evidence preservation, information sharing among governments and cable operators, and legal claims against responsible vessels, owners, insurers, or companies. Such a framework would formalise evidence preservation, incident notification deadlines, flag-state responsibilities, insurer obligations, operator information sharing, and compensation procedures. Accountability should be specific and evidence-based, targeting responsible vessels, companies, owners, insurers, or networks where evidence supports such action, not treating every cable fault as a war signal. Bounded accountability offers a middle path: respond firmly where evidence exists but preserve space for investigation before escalation. Backup connectivity as a crisis buffer Taiwan needs layered backup communications. Satellite and microwave systems cannot fully replace submarine cables, but they can keep essential communications alive during a crisis. Taiwan’s Ministry of Digital Affairs has already launched a non-geostationary orbit satellite verification project covering Taiwan’s main island as well as Kinmen, Matsu, Penghu, and Lanyu, including tests of medium Earth orbit and low Earth orbit capabilities. A more dispersed emergency communications architecture could include protected ground facilities, backup terminals, limited microwave redundancy for nearby islands, and deployable mobile systems reserved for essential public functions. This should be treated not as a substitute for submarine cables, but as a crisis buffer that gives investigators more time and policymakers more options. Taiwan’s undersea cables are therefore a test of whether the Indo-Pacific can manage grey-zone infrastructure risks without turning every disruption into a military crisis. The main challenge is not simply how to deter China, but how to respond in a way that is firm, evidentiary, and controlled. The right response is not escalation by default, but resilience by design: better evidence, faster repair, clearer rules, and limited backup connectivity. For Taiwan, this would reduce vulnerability without relying entirely on military signalling. For the wider Indo-Pacific, it would offer a model for managing infrastructure risks in contested maritime spaces. And for the US and its allies, it would demonstrate the discipline that grey-zone competition requires: the ability to respond without overreacting, and to protect partners without widening the path to war. article.content: Taiwan’s undersea cables are an Indo-Pacific crisis test Taiwan’s Undersea Cables Are an Indo-Pacific Crisis Test WRITTEN BY JING GE 12 June 2026 Taiwan’s undersea cables are not only a communications vulnerability; they are also a test of crisis discipline in the Indo-Pacific. In April 2026, poor weather conditions displaced wreckage off the coast of Taiwan’s remote Dongyin Island, severing an undersea cable . While backup microwave communications preserved basic connectivity, the incident revealed a deeper problem: in a Taiwan Strait crisis, a severed cable could be read as an accident, a coercive signal, or the opening move in a larger confrontation. The strategic risk lies not only in the cut itself, but in the ambiguity that follows. This is why Taiwan’s cable vulnerability should not be treated simply as another US-China flashpoint. It is a test of whether the US, Taiwan, and their Indo-Pacific partners can respond to grey-zone pressure without overreacting to every incident as an act of war. The challenge is to make cable coercion less effective while preserving the time and evidence needed to prevent escalation. Ambiguity is the real risk Taiwan’s digital connectivity rests on a relatively limited cable system. It has 25 submarine cables in total: 15 international links connecting Taiwan to Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Singapore, and the US, and 10 domestic inter-island cables linking the main island with Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu. For Taiwan’s outlying island communities, backup connections remain limited. If one break leaves an island offline for days or weeks, political pressure to respond can rise faster than investigators can determine what happened. The main challenge is not simply how to deter China, but how to respond in a way that is firm, evidentiary, and controlled. The right response is not escalation by default, but resilience by design: better evidence, faster repair, clearer rules, and limited backup connectivity. In early 2025, Taiwan experienced several undersea cable disruptions that raised concerns about whether accidents, negligence, or grey-zone activity were responsible. One serious case involved the Trans-Pacific Express cable, a key link connecting Taiwan with Asia and the US. Taiwanese authorities allege that a foreign-registered vessel operated by a Hong Kong company and crewed by Chinese nationals disabled its tracking system before dragging its anchor across the cable. Two further incidents followed: Taiwan’s Coast Guard reported a suspected attempted cable-cutting incident involving a Mongolia-flagged ship, and the Togo-flagged Hongtai 58 was linked to damage to the cable between Taiwan’s main island and Penghu. Determining responsibility for these vessels is challenging because they often operate in ways that complicate their activities: sailing under flags of convenience, changing names or registrations, masking beneficial ownership, switching off tracking systems, or claiming accidental anchoring. While such incidents may remain technical or legal matters in less contested waters, they can quickly take on deeper strategic significance in the Taiwan Strait. Hence, the risk is not only that cables may be cut, but that governments may feel compelled to respond before evidence is conclusive. China’s role makes this problem harder to separate from the region’s wider infrastructure competition. China is not only a military actor in the Taiwan Strait but also an increasingly important player in the Indo-Pacific’s digital and maritime infrastructure. Although Chinese firms such as HMN Technologies and China Unicom operate as commercial providers of digital connectivity and submarine-cable infrastructure, their projects exist within a broader strategic environment in which cable construction, data routes, port access, maritime presence, and political influence increasingly overlap. HMN Technologies has participated in multiple Indo-Pacific undersea cable projects, while Chinese-backed systems such as the Pakistan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE) cable show how cable routes can connect Asia, Africa, and Europe while reducing dependence on Western-controlled jurisdictions. This does not mean every cable fault around Taiwan should be treated as a Chinese operation. Over-attribution would be dangerous. But under-attribution also carries costs. If China or China-linked actors can exploit ambiguity, flags of convenience, and commercial cover to create pressure while avoiding responsibility, then Taiwan’s cable system becomes a grey-zone vulnerability. The real problem is the political space between accident and attack, where coercion can operate before attribution is settled. Evidence, repair, and rules The response should begin with shared attribution rather than automatic escalation. Taiwan, the US, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Australia, and relevant commercial operators should develop a regional monitoring and notification mechanism that creates a shared factual record before political narratives outrun evidence. Such a mechanism would not need to be militarised. It could combine the Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel identification, satellite imagery, maritime patrol records, port data, and cable operator information to determine whether a vessel loitered unusually in a cable zone, disabled its tracking system, changed identity or flag registration, or repeatedly appeared in high-risk areas. The aim should not be instant accusation, but evidence preservation and crisis control. Repair capacity is equally important. Cable disruption becomes more politically dangerous when restoration takes too long. If an outlying island loses connectivity for days or weeks, public pressure will grow, and governments may feel compelled to frame the incident in security terms. But if service can be restored quickly, the incident is more likely to remain within technical, legal, and law-enforcement channels. Repair ships, spare parts, emergency repair agreements, regional repair ports, and cooperation with commercial operators may sound less dramatic than military signalling, but they directly reduce the coercive value of disruption. The faster Taiwan can restore connectivity, the less useful cable cutting becomes as a tool of pressure. A third requirement is bounded accountability. Taiwan has already moved to treat submarine cables as critical infrastructure. In 2025, Taiwan’s Executive Yuan approved draft amendments involving seven laws, including the Telecommunications Management Act, the Electricity Act, the Natural Gas Enterprise Act, the Water Supply Act, the Meteorological Act, the Commercial Port Act, and the Ships Act, to strengthen protection for submarine cables, pipelines, and related infrastructure. Taiwan has also discussed stronger penalties for damaging submarine cables and measures allowing the government to seize related vessels or equipment in cases of illegality. The next step is to connect domestic protection with regional and international standards. In practice, a regional protocol should establish common rules for incident reporting, evidence preservation, information sharing among governments and cable operators, and legal claims against responsible vessels, owners, insurers, or companies. Such a framework would formalise evidence preservation, incident notification deadlines, flag-state responsibilities, insurer obligations, operator information sharing, and compensation procedures. Accountability should be specific and evidence-based, targeting responsible vessels, companies, owners, insurers, or networks where evidence supports such action, not treating every cable fault as a war signal. Bounded accountability offers a middle path: respond firmly where evidence exists but preserve space for investigation before escalation. Backup connectivity as a crisis buffer Taiwan needs layered backup communications. Satellite and microwave systems cannot fully replace submarine cables, but they can keep essential communications alive during a crisis. Taiwan’s Ministry of Digital Affairs has already launched a non-geostationary orbit satellite verification project covering Taiwan’s main island as well as Kinmen, Matsu, Penghu, and Lanyu, including tests of medium Earth orbit and low Earth orbit capabilities. A more dispersed emergency communications architecture could include protected ground facilities, backup terminals, limited microwave redundancy for nearby islands, and deployable mobile systems reserved for essential public functions. This should be treated not as a substitute for submarine cables, but as a crisis buffer that gives investigators more time and policymakers more options. Taiwan’s undersea cables are therefore a test of whether the Indo-Pacific can manage grey-zone infrastructure risks without turning every disruption into a military crisis. The main challenge is not simply how to deter China, but how to respond in a way that is firm, evidentiary, and controlled. The right response is not escalation by default, but resilience by design: better evidence, faster repair, clearer rules, and limited backup connectivity. For Taiwan, this would reduce vulnerability without relying entirely on military signalling. For the wider Indo-Pacific, it would offer a model for managing infrastructure risks in contested maritime spaces. And for the US and its allies, it would demonstrate the discipline that grey-zone competition requires: the ability to respond without overreacting, and to protect partners without widening the path to war. Additionally, some core wires of the Taima No. 2 submarine cable were damaged about 180 kilometers from Shalun in Tamsui, but the remaining core wires are sufficient for use during Matsu's peak hours and will not affect normal communications. Chunghwa Telecom reported that the cable was successfully reopened yesterday, and Dongyin's communication services have resumed transmission via submarine cables. The Ministry of Digital Affairs pointed out that on October 7 last year, the Taima-2 submarine cable experienced partial core wire damage at about 180 kilometers from Shalun in Tamsui. The remaining core wire is sufficient for peak use in Matsu and will not affect normal communications. If conditions permit, repairs are expected to be possible as early as November 30 this year.
